sections.title: The Dream and Its Sources
sections.html:
A dream is a story or a picture that a person sees and experiences in his sleep. The dream is registered in consciousness as something the person sees, and sometimes it is also registered as something he hears and touches. The dream appears without the person having any ability to choose it, and without his having any ability to control its course. Thus a person sometimes experiences a nightmare in his dream without being able to change it for the better. Sometimes a person sees himself in his dream doing terrible deeds, without his power of judgement being able to choose to prevent it. Admittedly, sometimes the nightmare stops when the person wakes from his dream in terror, but he was not able to change the course of the story in his dream for the better.

Apparently most dreams are forgotten, and a person remembers only dreams that he dreamt close to waking, or that left such an impression on his soul that they caused him to wake. Even those he generally forgets a short time after waking from sleep, and only those that left a particularly great impression on him does he remember even after several hours. However, people who are accustomed to attributing importance to their dreams also remember dreams that others regard as insignificant and forget in the blink of an eye. Therefore in periods and places in which people tended to attribute great importance to their dreams as foretelling the future or revealing hidden things, people remembered their dreams more, and would turn to dream interpreters so that they would decipher for them what they had seen in their dream.

Dreams stem from various sources. There are dreams about which the Sages said (Berakhot 55b): "A person is shown only what comes from the thoughts of his heart." As they related about the king of Persia, who turned to the Amora Shmuel and said: 'You claim that you are very wise; tell me what I will see in my dream tonight.' He answered him: 'You will see that your enemies, the Romans, take you captive, and you work for them at hard labour, grinding date pits in a mill of gold.' All day long he thought about it, and at night he saw this in his dream (ibid. 56a). One may not foretell the future on the basis of such dreams, and so it is stated (Zekharya 10:2): "For the terafim (idols) have spoken iniquity, and the diviners have seen a lie, and they tell false dreams; they comfort in vain."

And there are dreams about which the Sages said (Berakhot 55b) that the dream has a higher source and is a kind of prophecy, as it is stated (Bamidbar 12:6): "In a dream I will speak with him." The Sages further said (Berakhot 57a [?]) that a dream contains one part in sixty of prophecy. And the Sages said (Zohar I 238a): "At first prophecy rested upon human beings … Once prophecy ceased from them, they would make use of a bat kol (heavenly voice). Now prophecy has ceased and the bat kol has ceased, and people make use only of dreams." Indeed, even in our days there are stories of people who saw in their dream what was going to happen to them, and sometimes they were warned in a dream to flee from a disaster about to befall them, and thanks to the dream they were saved.1

sections.title: The Meaning of the Dream and Its Components
sections.html:
When a person is awake he controls his consciousness, and everything he perceives passes through the test of the intellect, which rejects anything that does not accord with the logic familiar to him. But during sleep he ceases to control his thought and imagination, and his soul is freed somewhat from the shackles of the body and of logic, and it can perceive imaginings from the depths of his soul and from higher worlds. Since the entire world unfolds from higher worlds, everything that is about to happen in the world is first known in a certain way in the higher worlds, and sometimes a person perceives something of this in his dream (see Derekh Hashem III 1:6).

The dream stems from three main components. (a) From events that happened to the person that day or in the recent past, and sometimes also from events that happened in the distant past and left an impression on his soul. This component is the basis of the story of the dream, as the Sages said that a person never dreamt of things that he had never seen at all in reality, such as an elephant passing through the eye of a needle (Berakhot 55b). (b) From various desires that the dreamer has, some good and some bad.

(c) From imaginings that a person perceives from the depths of his soul, or from the depths of the general human soul, or from higher worlds. Hidden in these imaginings are hints about the future and about hidden things. There is no disconnection between the depths of a person's soul, the depths of the general human soul and the higher worlds, for a person's soul parallels the general human soul and all the worlds. Therefore, the deeper a person delves into his soul, the more he correspondingly delves to some extent into the hidden recesses of the general human soul, and in the process he can reach a parallel perception in the higher worlds. And since the future events about to come into the world are already present as an idea in the higher worlds, in the depths of his soul he can sense this and perceive it through the imagination in a dream.

The Sages further explained (Berakhot 55b) that these imaginings, which come from the depths of the soul and from the higher worlds, sometimes come through angels and sometimes through demons. When dreams come through angels they tend more toward truth, as it is stated (Bamidbar 12:6): "In a dream I will speak with him"; and when they come through demons they tend more toward falsehood, as it is stated (Zekharya 10:2): "And they tell false dreams." That is to say, the more a person's soul is rectified of sins and distortions, the more he tends to receive dreams through an angel, that is, through a rectified spiritual force. And a person whose soul has been blemished by sins and distortions tends to receive dreams through a demon, that is, through a spiritual force that is not rectified, and then they are words of falsehood (see above, 17:5; 26, note 10).

However, since the dream is perceived in the personal imagination, with all its distortions and limitations, it never paints an accurate picture, to the point that the Sages said (Berakhot 55b [?]): "It is impossible to have a dream without idle matters." Only prophecy, which is given by the Lord in a manner suited to the prophet's imagination, can be perceived accurately.2

sections.title: Interpreting the Dream as Foretelling the Future
sections.html:
Since most of the components of a dream are based on events that happened to the person in the past or on various desires in his soul, the reliability of the dream is very low. Even a dream that is essentially true, since it is a dream, necessarily also has untrue things mixed into it, as the Sages said (Berakhot 55a): "Just as it is impossible to have grain without straw (chaff, which is waste), so it is impossible to have a dream without idle matters." Therefore, even when the dream is true, "although part of it is fulfilled, all of it is not fulfilled," as Yosef dreamt (Bereshit 37:9): "And behold, the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me." The sun alluded to his father, the moon to his mother, and the stars to his brothers; but at that time his mother had already died, and it was not possible for her to bow down to him.

Although as a rule the predictive value of a dream is very low, since man by nature longs to know the future, many were accustomed to seek an interpretation of their dream from dream interpreters. Even when the dream clearly described what was going to happen, they did not rely on it, for generally the dream taken literally is not correct, and only those with a special talent for interpreting dreams sometimes succeeded in extracting from the dream its kernel of truth and deciphering its meaning, and thereby foretelling the future. It is worth noting that most dream interpreters were not considered Torah scholars or righteous people. And those great figures of Israel who were known as interpreters of dreams, such as Yosef and Daniel, were aided by the holy spirit in interpreting the dreams. As Yosef said to the officers who found no interpretation for their dream: "Do not interpretations belong to God? Tell it to me, please" (Bereshit 40:8). Likewise, when Pharaoh said to Yosef: "And I have heard it said of you that you hear a dream and can interpret it," Yosef answered: "It is not in me" – the matter does not depend on me – rather, "God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace" (Bereshit 41:15-16).

And although the Sages of Israel were not known as professional dream interpreters, there are symbols whose meaning was known in Israel, and the Sages cited them in the Talmud (Berakhot 56b; 57a-b). However, it is difficult to make use of this in our days, because our language and our world of concepts are different, and the interpretation of a dream depends on the language and the world of concepts of that place and time. As the Sages said (Berakhot 56b), one who sees a cat in his dream: in a place where it is called 'shunra', it is a sign that a pleasant song ('shira na'ah') will be made for him; and in a place where it is called 'shinra', it is a sign that a bad change ('shinui ra') will be made for him. The place also affects the interpretation of a dream: one who sees himself naked in his dream – in Babylonia it is a sign that he is without sin; in the Land of Israel it is a sign that he is without mitzvot (Berakhot 57a). The person too affects the interpretation of the dream: an ordinary person who saw wine in his dream – sometimes it is a good sign for him and sometimes a bad sign, but for a Torah scholar it is always a good sign (ibid.). The season of the year also has an effect: a person who saw himself wearing a crown of olive leaves at the time the olives are growing will rise to greatness, and if he saw this at the time they are beaten [from the tree], he will be beaten (Yerushalmi Ma'aser Sheni 4:6).

sections.title: The Power of the Interpreter
sections.html:
The Sages further taught (Berakhot 55b): "All dreams follow the mouth," as it is stated (Bereshit 41:13): "And it came to pass, as he interpreted to us, so it was." Likewise Rabbi Bena'a related: "There were twenty-four dream interpreters in Jerusalem. Once I dreamt a dream and went to all of them, and what one interpreted for me the other did not interpret for me – and all of them were fulfilled in me." That is to say, the dream interpreter does not merely decipher the dream; rather, through the interpretation he utters with his mouth, he creates the process of its fulfilment – provided that the interpretation corresponds to the dream (Berakhot 55b), and also sits well with the heart of the dreamer (Ḥida, Ḥomat Anakh, Miketz 2).

That is to say, the interpretation affects the fulfilment of the dream, both because the dreamer accepts it, so that it is like a self-fulfilling prophecy, and because, although the dream does express something about to be fulfilled, it is still open to different directions, for hidden within it are many possibilities and meanings from the inner world of the dreamer and from the higher worlds, and the interpretation paves the way for the fulfilment of the dream in the world. For example, if the dream expressed a desire for wisdom, for rule or for marriage, there is reason to assume that this desire will seek to awaken and exert influence, and when the interpreter interprets it in a certain direction, he thereby charts the path to its fulfilment.

The Sages related (Berakhot 56a) about Bar Hedya, who was known as a great dream interpreter. In time it became clear that for anyone who paid him money he interpreted the dream favourably, and for anyone who did not pay him money he interpreted it unfavourably. Abaye and Rava used to go to him, and although they dreamt the same dreams, Abaye's dreams – since he paid him – he interpreted favourably, and Rava's dreams – since he did not pay him – he interpreted unfavourably. Once Bar Hedya's book fell into Rava's hands, and he found written in it: "All dreams follow the mouth," and he understood that through his bad interpretation he had caused him many troubles. Rava prayed that Bar Hedya be punished, and so it was that he was punished with a harsh death.

From this we learn that it is better for a person who dreamt a dream not to go to a dream interpreter; for since the dream follows the mouth, why should he go to an interpreter? As the Sages said (Berakhot 55b [?]): a dream that has not been interpreted is like a letter that has not been read; consequently, even if it was meant to foretell evil, by not being interpreted it is nullified. Admittedly, there are dreams that announce true things that do not depend on the interpreter, and one might have thought that in order to understand them it is worthwhile to go to a dream interpreter. However, even these it is better not to interpret. Instead, it is better to be aroused by them to strengthen oneself in the service of the Lord, as the Sages instructed (see section 7), and this will be the best interpretation for them. In any case, even one who decides to go to a dream interpreter should take care to go to a wise and good interpreter, so that he will interpret the dream for him favourably.3

sections.title: The Halakhic Attitude Toward Reality Revealed in a Dream
sections.html:
As halakha, generally one does not take the words of dreams into account, because most of them are nonsense. As the Sages said (Sanhedrin 30a): if a person knew that his late father had hidden money but did not know where he had put it, and in his sleep his father or the angel of dreams revealed itself to him and said: This money that you sought is located in such-and-such a place, and it contains such-and-such a sum, but you cannot use it because it belongs to so-and-so, or because it was consecrated as 'ma'aser sheni' – even though the son found the exact sum in the place he was told in the dream, he need not give the money to so-and-so or be concerned that it is 'ma'aser sheni'. For the Sages said: "The words of dreams neither raise nor lower" (SA ḤM 255:9). They further explained, on the basis of the words of the Sages, "It is impossible to have a dream without idle matters" (Berakhot 55a), that we attribute what his father told him – that the money belongs to so-and-so or is ma'aser sheni – to the idle matters in the dream (Meiri and Torat Ḥayim on Sanhedrin there).

However, if a person saw in his dream that he was being placed under a ban (nidui), since there is concern that he was banned by Heaven, and if so he has thereby entered into danger, he requires annulment. This annulment must be before ten Torah scholars, for the annulment must be like the ban: just as he was banned from Heaven, the place where the Shekhina rests, so they should annul the ban for him with ten, for the Shekhina rests upon ten of Israel. Even if in that same dream the ban was also annulled for him, he requires annulment before ten, for perhaps the ban is true and the annulment is among the idle matters in the dream (Nedarim 8a; SA 334:35).4

sections.title: Guidance and Halakhot in a Dream
sections.html:
Like all human beings, righteous Torah scholars too have dreams, and since they are occupied with Torah, mitzvot and good deeds, their dreams too are about these, for we learned (section 2) that dreams are based on events that happened to a person. We further learned (ibid.) that the more a person's soul is rectified of the blemishes of sins and bad character traits, the more his dreams come through angels and not demons, that is, through rectified rather than blemished spiritual forces, and consequently there is more truth in them and they are more understandable. However, since this is a dream, which necessarily also contains idle matters, the Sages took it into account only if it accorded with the guidance of Torah and ethics; and the more inspiration they merited to receive from it to strengthen themselves in the service of the Lord, the more they took it into account.

For example, Rabbi Moshe of Coucy used to travel among the communities of Israel and spread Torah, and several times he was asked to compose a book on all the mitzvot, but he did not consider himself worthy of it. Until he received a dream, as he wrote: "At the beginning of the sixth millennium (5001), a matter of a vision came to me in a dream: 'Arise, make a Torah scroll of two parts.' And I contemplated the vision, and behold, the two parts were to write the book of positive commandments in one part and the book of negative commandments in a second part." Thus he was aroused to write his book, the Semag – 'Sefer Mitzvot Gadol' (general introduction to the section on negative commandments). Likewise, there were Sages who issued a halakhic ruling following a dream, such as Rabbi Menaḥem Recanati, who following a dream understood that when taking the lulav it is proper to bring the etrog close to the three species, and the poskim cited his words as halakha (Beit Yosef OḤ 651:12; Taz 14). Likewise one of the great figures of the generations, the Radbaz (Rabbi David ben Zimra), related that he was asked whether it is permitted to make Rashi tefillin from Rabbeinu Tam tefillin, and he permitted it, but in his dream he saw that he had not ruled well, and he studied the topic again and retracted (Responsa Radbaz VI 2286). The Radbaz further wrote that during his sleep he would engage in halakhic deliberation, "and several times some of my doubts were resolved for me in a dream" (Migdal David on Shir Ha-shirim, on the verse "causing the lips of those who are asleep to speak"). And Rav Efrayim of Regensburg (a student of Rabbeinu Tam) at first held like the view of those who permit the barbuta fish, but he saw in his dream that they brought before him a bowl full of creeping creatures to eat, and he became angry. The master of the dream answered him: Why are you angry? Are you not the one who permits it! And he was angry at the answer. Thereupon he woke and remembered that he had permitted the barbuta that day, and he rose from his bed and broke the pots and bowls in which they had eaten (Or Zarua IV, Piskei Avoda Zara 200).

There were pious people who even made preparations and directed their intentions in order to receive answers to their questions in a dream. The most famous of them is Rabbi Ya'akov of Marvege, one of the Tosafists, who, when he sought an answer to his question, would seclude himself in his home and make preparations, and would receive in his dream brief answers by allusion. Sometimes he did not understand the allusion, and he asked again and received a certain elaboration. The answers he received were collected in the book 'Responsa Min Ha-shamayim' (Responsa from Heaven). And there were pious people who even adjured angels with holy names to reveal themselves to them in a dream and answer their questions. On the other hand, many opposed adjuring angels by names, out of concern that one who does so makes use of the crown of the Omnipresent without the proper honour (above, 20:3-4). As Sefer Ḥasidim (205) wrote: "One who engages in adjurations of angels or of demons … his end will not be good, and he will see evils in his body or in his children all his days. Therefore a person should keep far from doing all these things, and should also refrain from dream questions (she'elot ḥalom) …"

From a halakhic standpoint, an opinion stated on the basis of a dream has no precedence over an opinion stated on the basis of study. Moreover, even the dreamer himself was not permitted to rule on the basis of the dream, for we learned (above, 17:9) that it is forbidden to rule even on the basis of prophecy and the holy spirit, as it is stated (Devarim 30:12): "It is not in heaven" (Temura 16a). Therefore, only if the one who received the dream was convinced, on the basis of his own Torah judgement, that what was revealed to him in the dream was correct halakhically, would he accept it, and it is his own opinion that is taken into account.5

sections.title: Bad Dreams and Good Dreams
sections.html:
It is proper for a person who saw a bad and frightening dream not to worry about it, as the Sages said: "The words of dreams neither raise nor lower" (Sanhedrin 30a). So too the great Amora Shmuel conducted himself (Berakhot 55b): when he dreamt bad dreams, he said that there was nothing to them, for "they tell false dreams" (Zekharya 10:2). And when he dreamt good dreams, he rejoiced and said that there was substance to them, as it is stated (Bamidbar 12:6): "In a dream I will speak with him."

However, if he can, it is good that he be aroused to repentance by the bad dream, for everything that happens to a person, including his dreams, is meant to arouse him to repentance and to strengthen him in his good path. Therefore, if he sees a bad dream, he should not worry about it, but rather be aroused to repentance and understand through it that his good life is not guaranteed, and that he must strive to choose good so that his life will be worthy and good in the eyes of God and man. And if he sees a good dream, he should be encouraged to continue to rise in Torah and mitzvot. The Sages said (Berakhot 55a): "Ḥelma bisha adif me-ḥelma taba" – a bad dream is preferable to a good dream, for through it a person is aroused more to repentance. Sometimes a bad dream also brings atonement for sins, for through the distress of his dream he receives his punishment. As the Sages said (Berakhot 55a): "Ḥelma bisha kashe mi-nagda" – a bad dream is harsher than lashes, "as it is stated (Kohelet 3:14): 'And God has made it so that they should fear before Him' – this is a bad dream."

Since a person sometimes suffers greatly from bad dreams, the Sages gave advice to one who wishes to be saved from them: that he go to sleep amid words of Torah, for "whoever satiates himself with words of Torah and goes to sleep is not given bad tidings" (Berakhot 14a). This is one of the aims of the Shema recited at bedtime. In addition, in order to merit good dreams, it is good to sleep amid the joy of a mitzva, just as prophecy would rest upon the prophets amid joy (Pesaḥim 117a).

A person who dreamt a good dream and wants it to be fulfilled should remember it and act toward its fulfilment, as Yosef did, who remembered his dreams and did not cease to believe that if he acted righteously and walked in the ways of his fathers, his dreams would be fulfilled. This is what is stated (Bereshit 42:9): "And Yosef remembered the dreams which he had dreamt about them" (Zohar I 199b). This is because a good dream is meant to chart a direction, and unless he remembers it and strives to fulfil it, it will not be fulfilled.6

sections.title: Improving a Dream for One Who Is Very Worried
sections.html:
As we learned in the previous section, a person who saw a bad dream need not worry about it, and certainly not when the dream dealt with what he had been thinking about during the day. But if he dreamt a bad dream about things he had not been thinking about, and his soul is troubled by it, and he is very worried about the bad dream that perhaps foretells calamity for him, the Sages suggested that he go to three of those who love him and improve his dream before them (hatavat ḥalom).

This is the order of the improvement: he should open and say: "I have seen a good dream." Even though the dream seems very bad, he should not detail it, but rather say "I have seen a good dream," for by this he begins to improve it, since even a bad dream can be interpreted favourably (above, section 4). And they should respond and say: "It is good and may it be good; may the Merciful One make it good; seven times may they decree upon you from Heaven that it be good – and it will be good." Afterwards he should say three verses in which turning is mentioned, such as (Tehillim 30:12): "You have turned my mourning into dancing for me; You have loosed my sackcloth and girded me with joy"; and three verses of redemption, such as (ibid. 55:19): "He has redeemed my soul in peace from the battle that was against me, for there were many with me"; and three verses of peace, such as (Yeshayahu 57:19): "I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to the far and to the near, says the Lord, and I will heal him" – as printed in the siddurim (Berakhot 55b; SA OḤ 220:1).

Another piece of advice for improving a bad dream is through prayer during Birkat Kohanim. And although this advice was stated regarding a dream about which it is not known whether it is good or bad (see below, section 10), since we do not know how to interpret dreams, even when the dream seems bad, one can regard it as an unclear dream and improve it through Birkat Kohanim.7

sections.title: A Fast for a Dream
sections.html:
Another way to nullify a bad dream is through fasting. The Sages said (Shabbat 11a): "A fast is as effective for a dream as fire is for tow," for when a person fasts and repents, the calamity he dreamt of is completely nullified. This fast must take place immediately after the bad dream, because if he was shown the dream on this day, there is concern that the decree depends on that day, and it is specifically on that day that it can be nullified. Therefore, even if he dreamt a bad dream on Friday night, he may fast on Shabbat in order to nullify it. But since by his fast he neglected the mitzva of delighting in Shabbat, he must atone for his fast with an additional fast, and he should try to fast right away on Sunday. If he is unable to fast on Sunday because he was weakened by the Shabbat fast, or because Sunday is a Yom Tov, he should fast as soon as possible in order to atone for having fasted on Shabbat (Shabbat 11a; Ta'anit 12b; SA OḤ 220:2; 288:4-5).

A fast for a dream (ta'anit ḥalom) is not an obligation, nor even a mitzva, but optional; therefore one who is not worried about his dream need not fast even on a weekday (Rashba 1:132; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 288:7; MB 220:7).

In practice, for several reasons, already in the days of the Rishonim fewer people fasted for a dream, and all the more so on Shabbat. First, some say that one fasts only for a bad dream seen three times (Mordekhai in the name of Maharam). Second, some say that it was customary to fast only for three particular bad dreams (Binyamin Ze'ev 211, in the name of Rav Hai Gaon). Third, if the dream is about something he thought about during the day, he need not worry about it (Maharsha; Taz 288:3; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 13). Fourth, already in the days of the Rishonim there were those who said that there is no one expert enough in dreams to know which dream is bad and requires a fast to nullify it (Rav Amram, and Ra'avya in the name of Rabbi Kalonymus), for the interpretation of a dream depends on the language and the world of concepts of that place (above, section 3).

So too the Aḥaronim wrote that just as remedies have changed from the period of the Gemara to our period (below, 29:5), so too the interpretation of dreams has changed; therefore only one whose soul is so troubled by the dream that he derives more delight from the fast than from the Shabbat meals may fast on Shabbat (Eliyahu Rabba 288:12; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 7; Da'at Torah 5). And even such a person it is better to persuade not to fast, as explained in the note. Instead, he should pray about it during Birkat Kohanim, as explained in the next section.[8]

sections.title: Prayer During Birkat Kohanim
sections.html:
The Sages said that one who saw a dream and does not know whether it is good or bad, and is worried about it, should, immediately the next day, during Birkat Kohanim, say a prayer for the improvement of the dream: "Master of the universe, I am Yours and my dreams are Yours. I have dreamt a dream and I do not know what it is – whether I dreamt about myself, or my companions dreamt about me, or I dreamt about others. If they are good, strengthen them and fortify them like the dreams of Yosef; and if they need healing, heal them like the waters of Mara through Moshe our teacher, and like Miriam from her leprosy, and like Ḥizkiyahu from his illness, and like the waters of Yeriḥo through Elisha. And just as You turned the curse of the wicked Bil'am into a blessing, so turn all my dreams for me to the good." He should try to finish his prayer with the conclusion of Birkat Kohanim, so that the response of 'Amen' to Birkat Kohanim will apply to his prayer as well (Berakhot 55b; SA OḤ 130:1). Even when it is clear to him that the dream is bad, he may say in the text of the prayer "I do not know what it is," for he does not know its meaning, and perhaps its interpretation is good. A kohen may say the prayer before he raises his hands or immediately after he raises his hands. After the text for improving the dream, many have the custom of saying 'Adir Ba-marom', which is printed in the siddurim (see Peninei Halakha, Tefila 20, note 1).

The time of Birkat Kohanim is suitable for improving a dream, because in Birkat Kohanim Israel are blessed with protection and peace, and thereby they are saved from calamities. The Sages said (Zohar III 147a-b, in translation): "At the time that the kohen raises his hands, the people must be in fear and awe, and know that at that time there is a time of favour in all the worlds, and the upper and lower beings are blessed, and there is no judgement in any of them … Whoever is distressed by his dream should come at the time that the kohanim spread their hands and say: Master of the universe, I am Yours and my dreams are Yours … For at that time there is mercy in all the worlds, and whoever prays his prayer over his distress, the judgement is turned for him into mercy."[9]
